about: Colonia (Cologne) on the Rhine: one port, written 6 October 2026 from Design/content/dossiers/colonia.md and the spine. A draft in the game's own files, for the user to overwrite. (?) marks what is not attested. No count, toll man, moneyer or merchant of Colonia is named in the sources: every named person here except the archbishops Hildebold, Hadebald and Bruno is the game's. Woven with the other ports of the region (Mogontia, Diusburg, Ganda, Andoverpis) on the same day: ties both ways, beats in each other's stories, and the cards of encounters/rhineland_flanders_793.json on the sites.

ports.summary: The old Roman city on the left bank of the Rhine, three to five days above Dorestad with the stream and ten to fifteen back against it. In 793 it is a bishop's seat inside a Roman wall of nineteen towers, with a strip of low ground between wall and river where boats lie and things are made. A merchant comes for Rhenish wine, the grey-yellow pots of the Vorgebirge villages, querns of black Mayen stone, glass and iron, and brings Frisian cloth, salt, fish and whatever the north sells.
ports.seasons: The vintage is in the weeks before Saint Gereon's day and the new wine is ready by Martinmas, when every hull on the river is wanted at once. The river is low in late summer and high with the snow water in spring; there is no tide and no bar, but in a hard winter the Rhine freezes and nothing moves for a month.

history.text: About this year the emperor Constantine joined the city to the fort of Deutz on the far bank by a bridge on stone piers with a timber deck, nearly three hundred paces long. Whether any of it stood in 793 is not known (?).
After this year Plectrude, Pippin's widow, died here and was buried in the church she had built on the mound of the old temple of Jupiter, Juno and Minerva.
This year Hildebold became bishop of Colonia. From 791 he was also the king's archchaplain, and was more often at court than in his city.
In this year or the next Colonia was made an archbishop's seat, set in time over Utrecht, Liège, Bremen, Minden, Münster and Osnabrück.
history.source: de.wikipedia Hildebold von Köln (dossier); the Saxon sees of Minden and Münster have bishops only from about 803-805 (?)

history.text: This year Archbishop Hildebold gave the dying emperor Charles the last rites at Aachen.
This year, on the third day of September, Hildebold died. He was buried at Saint Gereon's outside the wall.
history.source: de.wikipedia Hildebold von Köln; St. Gereon (dossier)

history.text: In the winter before this year the Rhine was frozen for thirty days, and carts crossed where boats had.
This year Harald, king of the Danes, newly baptised, and the monk Anskar took boat here for Dorestad. Bishop Hadebald gave them a good boat with two cabins.
This year the books of Saint Peter's were listed: one hundred and seventy-five.
history.source: de.wikipedia Erzbischöfliche Diözesan- und Dombibliothek Köln (dossier)

history.text: This year the kingdom was parted in three and Colonia fell to Lothar's middle share; in 855 to the second Lothar; in 870 to the eastern king.
This year King Louis came to Colonia by boat.

This year, on the fifteenth day of September, in a great storm the people ran into Saint Peter's and rang the bells. Lightning like a fiery dragon split the church and killed a priest, a deacon and a layman at three altars.
This year in October the pope put Archbishop Gunthar out of his office over King Lothar's divorce. He went on acting as archbishop regardless.

This year Willibert was ordained archbishop on the seventh of January at King Louis's order, and on the twenty-sixth or twenty-seventh of September Saint Peter's was dedicated. The night before, evil spirits were heard grieving that they must leave seats they had held so long.

This year Charles, the western king and since Christmas emperor, sat at Colonia with his army. Archbishop Willibert sent the priest Hartwig to warn the younger Louis, who beat Charles at Andernach on the eighth of October.

In the winter of this year the Northmen burned Colonia and Bonn with their churches and buildings. The clergy fled to Mainz with the treasures and the bodies of the saints. A ransom paid in January did not save the town.
history.source: Annales Fuldenses 881 (ed. Kurze 1891); de.wikipedia Raubzüge der Wikinger in das Rheinland. Digs have not found the burning.

history.text: This year Colonia was rebuilt, without its churches and monasteries, and its walls restored with gates, bars and locks. The Northmen went by.
This year Archbishop Hermann asked the pope for relics to replace those that had burned.
This year a market of Colonia is first named in writing, and in the same year nuns from Gerresheim, fleeing the Hungarians, came to the church of the Holy Virgins.
This year Bruno, King Otto's brother, became archbishop and duke of Lotharingia; from his day the archbishop held court, market, mint and toll. He died on the eleventh of October 965.
history.source: de.wikipedia Brun (Köln); Geschichte der Stadt Köln (dossier)

history.text: About this year the hay market by the river was first laid, by the date of its timbers; about 960 Bruno set a chapter at Saint Martin's on the old island.
This year at Christmas Heribert entered the town barefoot as archbishop. In 1003 he founded an abbey in the old fort of Deutz across the river.
history.source: de.wikipedia Heribert von Köln; Kastell Deutz (dossier)

history.text: About this year the men of the emperor who came to London in their own ships paid toll there, and at Christmas and Easter two grey cloths and a brown one, ten pounds of pepper, five men's gloves and two casks of vinegar. The men of Colonia are usually counted among them (?).
history.source: IV Æthelred 2 (Thorpe, Ancient Laws 1840); the code may be later than it claims

history.text: This year Pope Leo consecrated an altar at Saint Mary's on the temple mound.
This year in April Archbishop Anno took the boy king at Kaiserswerth. The boy jumped from the ship into the Rhine, was pulled out by Count Ekbert, and was brought to Colonia.

eras.text: Hildebold's years. The bishop is the king's archchaplain and seldom at home; his clerks run the church's business and hold the king's lists. Inside the wall are gardens, ruins and churches; the trade is outside it, on the low ground by the river, among pit houses, smiths, glass workers and bone workers. Pennies of King Charles are struck. In the hungry years the king's grain comes down the river, and in 799 and 804 Saxon families wait on the bank to be sent into Francia.

Hadebald's years. A church of Saint Peter has burned and is building again. The river is busy and safe as far as anyone here knows. In 826 a Danish king goes down it in the bishop's boat. The books of Saint Peter's are counted and lent.

The middle kingdom's years. Whose town this is changes four times in a lifetime, and the archbishop's chair is quarrelled over by kings and the pope. Dorestad is raided year after year and its merchants come upriver to ask about plots. The great church with a choir at each end is dedicated in 870.

The burning. The Northmen winter on the lower river, take a ransom and burn the town anyway. The clergy are at Mainz with the saints. People live in what is left against the wall, the strand is bare of boats, and nothing is sold that cannot be carried off in a hurry.

Rebuilt behind mended walls with gates, bars and locks. The river suburb grows again; by 922 its market has a name in writing, and the pennies read S COLONIA A. Nuns from Gerresheim keep the church of the Holy Virgins. The fine painted pots now come from Pingsdorf.

Bruno's town and his successors': the archbishop is lord of court, market, mint and toll. The river suburb is taken inside the walls. There is a chapter at Saint Martin's on the old island, with Irish monks before the century is out, and an abbey at Saint Pantaleon. Gero's great oak cross hangs in Saint Peter's.

The largest town on the Rhine, of some ten thousand people. Its merchants own sea-going ships and are known in London as the emperor's men. Heribert's abbey stands in the fort at Deutz. Under Anno the archbishop's hand is heavy, and the merchants have begun to say so to each other.

sites.name: The strand under the wall
sites.see: A long shelf of gravel and trodden mud between the brown river and a Roman wall eight metres high, its towers patterned in coloured stone. Flat river boats lie nose-in with planks run ashore; tow ropes dry on stakes. Gulls, hammering from the smiths, and the smell of wet rope, dung and wood smoke.
sites.source: The east wall faces the river across low ground that was the Roman harbour, silted since the 2nd and 3rd centuries (de.wikipedia Alter Markt; CCAA). Boats most likely lay along it; no quay is recorded (?).

sites.name: The market on the old harbour ground
sites.see: An open stretch of dark trampled earth between low thatched pit houses. In front, tall pale jars with bands of clay ribbon stand in straw, casks lie on their sides, and black querns are stacked like loaves. Behind, the wall and the roofs of the bishop's church. Smoke, sour wine lees, pigs.
sites.source: Pit houses of the 5th to 7th centuries and a dark layer of dung, bone and craft waste under the later markets (the Heumarkt dig (?)); 'mercatus coloniae' is first written in 922, 'forum' in 988 (de.wikipedia Alter Markt). Badorf jars up to 70 cm for wine and oil (de.wikipedia Badorfer Keramik).

sites.name: The river gate
sites.see: A Roman gate in the east wall, one of its arches walled up with rubble, the other worn smooth at cart-axle height. A bench, a balance on a post, and a clerk with a wax tablet in the shade. Beyond the arch a straight paved street runs uphill between gardens and broken walls.
sites.source: Nine Roman gates (de.wikipedia CCAA). No toll rate and no toll man is recorded before 1066 (?): the bench is the game's. From 953 the toll is the archbishop's (de.wikipedia Brun).

sites.name: The king's mint
sites.see: A stone room built into a Roman cellar near the bishop's hall, lit by a charcoal hearth. A man sets a blank on an iron die fixed in a block, lays the upper die on it and strikes once. On the table: a small balance, a pan of clipped old pennies, a touchstone.
sites.source: Pennies of Charles for Colonia, 771-794 (seen only in a search summary (?)); the S COLONIA A type from Louis the Child (900-911) to Henry II (Münze des Monats, Münster, July 2017). Where the mint stood is not known (?). No moneyer is named: the pennies name king and city.

sites.name: Saint Peter's
sites.see: The bishop's church in the north-east corner of the walls: a long plain stone hall with a tiled roof, half of it under scaffolding in most years. Inside it is cold and lamp-lit; boys chant at the east end and a scribe sits in the light of a west window with a book chest beside him.
sites.source: A church of about 800 burned some ten years later; the great church with a choir at each end was dedicated in 870 or 873, its nave 97.5 m (de.wikipedia Hildebold-Dom). 175 books listed in 833. From about 970 the Gero Cross hangs mid-nave (de.wikipedia Gerokreuz).

sites.name: The smiths' row
sites.see: A lane of open-fronted sheds along the foot of the wall, each with a hearth, a stone anvil block and a boy at the bellows. Scythe blades, knives and boat nails hang in bunches. At the far end a shed is closed with hurdles, and it is the only quiet one. Charcoal, hot iron, scorched horn.
sites.source: Waste of metal, glass and bone working by the river (the Heumarkt dig (?)); swords among the Rhine's exports (Design/economy_and_trade.md). The row and the closed shed are the spine's (swords_north). The ban on selling mail outside the realm: Capitulary of Herstal 779 c. 20.

sites.name: The boat bank below Saint Kunibert's
sites.see: North of the wall the bank shelves gently under a small stone church. A flat-bottomed barge sits on rollers with her side planks off; two men split an oak log with wedges, and moss and tar for caulking wait in a trough. Chips underfoot, the sweet smell of green oak, a tar pot smoking.
sites.source: Saint Kunibert's on the bank north of the walls (de.wikipedia St. Kunibert). River craft; hired rowers in 1062 and merchants with their own ships in 1074 (de.wikipedia Anno II.). No yard is recorded (?): placing it here is the game's.

sites.name: The Deutz crossing
sites.see: A broad ferry of planks worked across the stream on sweeps, landing under the square stone fort of Deutz on the far side, eighteen towers against the morning light. At low water grey stumps of masonry show in a line across the river where the Romans' bridge stood (?). Wind, horses stamping on the deck.
sites.source: The fort of Deutz, 142 m square with 18 towers, a royal estate; Heribert's abbey in it from 1003 (de.wikipedia Kastell Deutz). The bridge of 310: whether any of it still stood is unknown (?). The Saxon families on the bank in 799 and 804 are the spine's placing (saxon_end).

sites.name: The ale-house in the tower
sites.see: The ground floor of a Roman wall tower on the river side, its doorway knocked through at strand level. A fire on a stone hearth in the middle, smoke going up into the hollow tower, benches round the curve of the wall, a tub of ale and a row of pale Badorf cups. Boatmen, a dice cup, a dog.
sites.source: Nineteen towers on the wall (de.wikipedia CCAA). The ale-house is the game's (?); people lived and worked on the river strip from the 5th century.

sites.name: The Golden Saints
sites.see: Outside the north-west corner of the wall, among Roman tombs and vegetable plots, an old oval hall of brick and stone with deep round niches. Inside, the vault still shows gold glass in patches where the lamp reaches. Graves crowd up to the walls outside. Quiet, crows, cold stone and wax.
sites.source: Saint Gereon: a late Roman oval hall of about 350-365, 'at the Golden Saints' in Gregory of Tours; Hildebold's grave from 818. Burial by the saints outside the walls in the old Roman cemeteries (de.wikipedia St. Gereon; St. Severin).

sites.name: Saint Mary's on the temple mound
sites.see: In the south of the town a church stands on a great squared platform of Roman stone higher than a man, reached by a ramp. From its door you look over the wall to the river and the boats. Inside, a plain stone coffin lies before the altar with a lamp that is never let go out.
sites.source: Plectrude's church and grave (she died after 717) on the podium of the Capitoline temple; rebuilt 1049-1065, its carved wooden doors survive (de.wikipedia St. Maria im Kapitol). Whether women kept the church and tended the sick there in 793 is not known (?).

sites.name: Saint Martin's on the island
sites.see: A new stone church and a cluster of timber buildings on the rise that was once an island in the Roman harbour, right above the market. Monks with their hair shaved across the front of the head in the old Irish way (?) go between church and guest house, speaking Latin with an accent nobody here can place.
sites.source: Bruno's chapter of about 960 over Roman warehouses; Irish abbots Minnborinus (died 986), Kilian (1003), Helias (1040), Aaron (1052), Molanus (1061); Marianus Scotus there about 1056 (en.wikipedia Great St. Martin Church; de.wikipedia Groß St. Martin). The two articles differ on when the Irish came. The Irish tonsure so late is a guess (?).

people.name: Hildebold
people.trait: The king's archchaplain: a court man, quick, well read, used to being obeyed without raising his voice. Home at Colonia only for the great feasts.
people.want: A church of Saint Peter worthy of an archbishop's seat, books to fill it, and his clerks left alone to keep the king's business in order.
people.fear: Fire in the church, and that he will die at court and be remembered only as the king's priest.
people.voice: Courteous and brief. Asks one exact question, listens to the whole answer, and has already decided.
people.looks: About fifty, lean, clean-shaven, a tonsure gone grey; a plain dark wool cloak over a long white tunic, a gold ring, and a small prayer book bound in deer hide in his hand.
knows: where the king is this season and where the host will go
what the synod at Frankfurt ruled on coin, measures and the price of bread (from 794)
which books Saint Peter's has and which it lacks
who has the churches at Traiectum, Mimigernaford and Bremen in his care, and what each of them wants carried

ties.note: raised him from a schoolboy and trusts him with the lists and the seal when he is at court
the old priest baptised half the river strip; Hildebold lets him say what clerks may not
fellow courtiers; in the court's game of names Hildebold is called Aaron
Liudger's Saxon and Frisian districts answer to Colonia; Hildebold consecrates him bishop here on 30 March 805
from 794 or 795 the bishop of Traiectum is his suffragan and gets his orders by river
Riculf of Mogontia holds the other great Rhine see and the older claim to be first
the steward at the Ruhr mouth gets the king's orders about the hostages from him, by river, and answers in numbers
the same Liudger, as he is met at the Ruhr mouth from 799: ordained priest at Colonia in 777 and consecrated bishop here by Hildebold on 30 March 805
the young abbot of Saint-Denis learns the court from him and has the archchaplain's place after him (?)

lines.greet: You are the Frisian with the small boat. My clerk says you pay what is asked and argue afterwards. That is the right order. What do you carry?
lines.greet_again: The boat from Dorestad again. Good. I have been at court since Easter and nobody there can tell me what a cask costs.
rumour: The king winters where the war is. If you want to sell grain or horses, ask where the host gathers in May, not where it was.
There is a new penny, heavier than the old. It is to be taken everywhere. I helped write that, so do not ask me to change it.
Fire is the enemy of an old church. I mean to build Saint Peter's in stone. If you see good lead for sale on the Thames, tell my clerk.
lines.saying: A man once asked me for a scrap of deer hide to bind a prayer book, when he could have had gold. I have thought better of him since.
lines.farewell: Go with God, and go before the water drops. Hrotbert will have a letter for Traiectum; it weighs nothing.

people.source: Bishop 787, archchaplain 791, archbishop 794/795, died 3 September 818 (de.wikipedia Hildebold von Köln). His birth year is not known. The deer-hide tale is a late legend, turned round here on purpose. His court name Aaron and his consecration of Liudger at Colonia on 30 March 805 are in the same article (checked 7 October 2026). The church he had about 800 burned some ten years later (de.wikipedia Hildebold-Dom): so he speaks of fire as a fear and of building as an intention, in any year.

people.name: Hrotbert
people.trait: The bishop's clerk for the mint, the gate and the king's lists: exact, tireless, fond of a rule he can read aloud.
people.want: Every penny on the river of one weight and every name on his lists accounted for, alive or dead.
people.fear: An error found in his lists by the king's envoys; worse, one found by nobody.
people.voice: Reads out the rule before he answers the question. Not unkind: he simply thinks the rule is the answer.
people.looks: About thirty, thin and stooped, ink on the right thumb, a clerk's tonsure; a grey tunic to the shin, a wax tablet and stylus hung at his belt, a ring of keys.
knows: the rate at which old pennies and foreign silver are taken at the mint, and the fine for refusing the new coin
the king's top prices for oats, barley, rye and wheat (from 794)
which Saxon hostages and families passed Colonia, in whose keeping and where they were sent
what the bishop wants carried downriver and what he pays

ties.note: his master and teacher; writes to him at court every week whether or not there is news
from 819 the new archbishop, whom he serves five years and corrects daily, on the ground that the lists were there first
they disagree about the Saxons and eat together every Sunday
knows what is behind the hurdles in the smiths' row and has never yet caught it leaving
the moneyer at Dorestad; they send each other bad pennies as other men send greetings
a name on his list of 785 is Brunger's brother; Hrotbert knows the entry and has not been asked the right way
sends the hostage lists on to the archbishop's clerks at Mogontia when the king orders it
the list-keeper at Mogontia: the hostage rolls go up to him and his corrections come down; they write to each other in lists and have never met
weighs every Mogontia penny that reaches his table and writes to the moneyer to say what he found; the moneyer weighs Colonia's
checks the steward's tallies against the king's price every Martinmas and has never yet found the error he is sure is there
takes the rent of the tower in ale and in what she chooses to overhear; knows she chooses, and is content with it
a poor priest on the Scheldt wants the same Life of Willibrord for his feast that Hrotbert wants for Saint Peter's chest; Hrotbert has offered the carrier a hundred and twenty pennies for it

lines.greet: Name, boat, where from. The new pennies are to be taken in every place, town and market. Now: what can I do for you?
lines.greet_again: Dorestad, the small boat, four men. You see, I keep you. Have you any old coin aboard? Better to tell me than the gate.
rumour: The king's price for a measure of wheat is four pennies and nobody may ask more. I did not say nobody does. I said nobody may.
Sigimar at Dorestad sent me a penny that is tin under the skin. From an English purse, he says. Test what you are given across the sea.
More Saxons are to come down to the crossing before harvest. Whole households. I am to count them. Nobody told me how they are to be fed.
lines.saying: A thing written down can still be wrong. But it is wrong in one place, where you can find it.
lines.farewell: Go safely. If you pass Traiectum, greet the bishop's clerk and tell him his sums of last year are a penny out.

people.source: invented; the office from the spine (silver_road, saxon_end): the archbishop's clerks keep the mint's rule and the king's lists. The rule he reads is Frankfurt 794 c. 5; the wheat price is Frankfurt 794 c. 4.

people.name: Erkanbert
people.trait: The old priest of the river strip and the graves outside the wall: blunt, tired, kind in a way that costs him.
people.want: That the Saxons he reads the vow to should be fed before they are preached at, and buried properly if they die on his bank.
people.fear: That a baptism got by the sword counts for nothing, and that he has done several hundred.
people.voice: Slow, plain, a countryman's Frankish. Says the hard thing first and softens it afterwards if at all.
people.looks: Near sixty, broad and red-faced, a white fringe round a bald crown; a patched brown cloak, muddy shoes, a wooden cross on a thong and a satchel with a book in it.
knows: the baptismal vow in the Saxons' own tongue, by heart
who lies in which grave at the Golden Saints, and the tale of the soldier saints
which households on the strand are hungry and which are hiding grain
what the Saxons on the bank say when the clerks are not listening

ties.note: his bishop; tells him to his face that the war makes bad Christians
the clerk counts the Saxons and the priest feeds them; neither thinks the other has the harder task
his sister's daughter; he drinks at her fire and pays in advice
thinks Liudger the only man who preaches to Saxons as if they could hear
read the vow over a boatload of Weser men in 785, Brunger and his brother among them, and remembers the two boys
the king's steward at the Ruhr mouth sends a boy up the river when a column is on the Hellweg, so that there is bread on the bank at Colonia before the people are (?)
read the vow over her band at the crossing in 785; she said the words in a girl's voice and looked at the river the whole time, and he has not forgotten her face

lines.greet: A Frisian. Good. You people at least were baptised a generation ago and have had time to get used to it. Have you bread to spare?
lines.greet_again: You came back. Most do not, once they have seen the bank on a bad day. Sit. Tell me what bread costs downriver.
rumour: They wait on the bank by households. I read them the vow again, in their own tongue. They say the words. I do not ask what they mean by them.
Your big Saxon will not look at me. I do not blame him. Tell him the old priest remembers two boys from the Weser, and is sorry.
The soldiers under the Golden Saints would not kill at the emperor's order, and were killed for it. I think of that, these years, more than I should.
lines.saying: You can make a man say he forsakes the devil. You cannot make him stop being hungry while he says it.
lines.farewell: God keep you on the water. If you carry any of them upriver, carry them gently. They are baptised, whatever else they are.

people.source: invented; the spine's priest at the crossing (saxon_end). The vow is the Old Saxon baptismal vow (texts_793.json saxon_vow). Gereon and the soldiers of the Theban Legion: de.wikipedia St. Gereon.

people.name: Meginher
people.trait: A dealer in querns and millstones from the Mayen pits: patient, heavy, thinks in boatloads and years.
people.want: To know what the English want before the ban is lifted, so that his stones are on the strand at Dorestad the week it is.
people.fear: A yard full of roughed-out stones cut to the wrong size, and a son who would rather sell wine.
people.voice: Unhurried. Pats whatever he is selling. Answers a question with what it will cost to answer.
people.looks: Mid-forties, thick-armed and grey with stone dust to the elbows, a full brown beard; a leather apron over a russet tunic, a measuring stick notched in hand-breadths.
knows: what a quern, a millstone and a roughout cost here and at Dorestad
which boats bring stone down from Andernach and when
that the king's order closed the English trade, and roughly why
who at Dorestad finishes stones and what they owe him

ties.note: his brother's widow; shares his pitch on the market and corrects his prices in front of buyers
ships his stones on the king's grain boats when they go down empty, and pays the steward in favours
the Dorestad skipper buys his stones on credit and sells the same news to both sides
stores his finished querns in her storehouse on the dam and has never been cheated by a handful
has never met the wic-reeve of Lundenwic, and would pay well for one true word from him
a Mogontia grain man who takes his millstones up to the Main mills (?)
lets the smith's long bundles ride under his querns to Dorestad, charges nothing for it, and has never asked what is in them
the quern-dresser on the Almere shore takes his roughouts on credit each spring and pays in dressed pairs; he is the stone dealer Tado means
the toll man on the Scheldt counts every quern that goes up to the abbeys at Ganda, aloud, twice, and takes the tenth in stones

lines.greet: Mayen stone. Black, light for its size, and it does not grit your bread. Lift one. You have been to England, have you? Sit down.
lines.greet_again: The man who crosses the sea. I kept a stone back for you. Tell me first what you heard on the Thames.
rumour: The English king asked our king for black stones. Nobody told me what size. I have two hundred roughouts and no idea where to cut.
At Dorestad the finished querns pile up unsold. Buy there cheap if you have somewhere to keep them. The quarrel of kings cannot last.
They say our king complains the English cloaks have got short. A king who measures cloaks will measure millstones next.
lines.saying: Wine is drunk in a year, a pot broken in two. A quern is sold once and grinds for the grandchildren. That is why I am not rich.
lines.farewell: Go well. And ask about the stones. A hand-breadth either way is a boatload wasted.

people.source: invented; the spine's stone dealer (black_stones). Mayen lava querns down the Rhine and finished at Dorestad (Research/dorestad_c800_notes.md). The black stones and the cloaks are in Charles's letter to Offa of 796; that the stones were querns is one reading of it (?).

people.name: Gerhild
people.trait: A potter's widow from the Vorgebirge who sells the villages' jars by the stack and fills them with wine for the north: sharp, funny, never short-measured.
people.want: Her son's kiln at Badorf kept burning, and one buyer in every northern market who asks for her mark.
people.fear: A wet autumn: a spoiled vintage and unfired pots in the same month.
people.voice: Fast and teasing. Names a price, then names the reason you will pay it.
people.looks: About forty, small and wiry, sleeves rolled, clay under the nails; a head cloth, a madder-red dress kilted up for work, a tasting cup on a cord at her waist.
knows: what Badorf jars, cups and pitchers cost by the cart, and what Rhenish wine costs by the cask and the season
which villages' kilns fire well this year
how to pack pots in straw so a boat can take a sea
the gossip of every hill village from here to Bonn

ties.note: her dead husband's brother; she thinks stone is a slow trade for a slow man, and says so
sells her the cups that boatmen break, at a price that assumes they will
the steward takes carts in the vintage weeks that she had bespoken
the widow on the dam at Dorestad is her buyer of twenty years; they have met twice
a Svea trader once paid her in advance for jars with a pattern of tin foil; she has not yet found the potter who can do it
the ferryman at the Ruhr mouth takes her seconds up the Ruhr for the inland farms and pays in smoked eels (?); no Frisian stays at that landing in her time
the Frisian wine shipper at Mogontia fills her tall jars for the north; she says the jar sells his wine and he says the wine sells her jar
Liutwin sells wine in the cask and glass to drink it from; she sells wine in the jar and clay to drink it from, on the next pitch, and louder
the ale-wife on the Scheldt drinks from her cups and stands her spouted pots by the vat; they know each other by the mark under the handle
the ale-wife at Ganda saw her grey pots come down from Valenciennes, the long way round, and sent word by a bargeman to ask who was selling to both rivers

lines.greet: You have a hold and I have pots. Knock on that one. Hear it ring? A cracked jar says nothing. Like a husband.
lines.greet_again: My Frisian. Did the last load reach Dorestad whole? No, do not tell me. Tell me how many you want this time.
rumour: The new wine is not ready till Martinmas, whatever the man by the casks says. Before that he is selling you last year's with a prayer.
A Northman at Dorestad asked for black jugs with tin leaves on them. I said: for that money I will stick the leaves on myself.
The tall jars with the ribbons go north full of wine and nobody sends them back. I ought to thank the heathen for their thirst.
lines.saying: The potter's own house eats off wood. Everything that rings is for sale.
lines.farewell: Straw between every two, and nothing heavy on top. If they break it is your steersman, not my clay.

people.source: invented; women trading in their own names are not attested (?), a potter's widow selling for the kiln is the game's. Badorf ware from Walberberg, Eckdorf and Badorf with Colonia its market and loading place (de.wikipedia Badorfer Keramik). The tin-foil jugs are Tating ware, found from Dorestad to Birka.

people.name: Wido
people.trait: Steward of the king's estate at Deutz: loud, honest in the king's interest, short of boats every year of his life.
people.want: Hulls. The king's grain moved before it sprouts, his wine moved before it turns, and a clean reckoning at Martinmas.
people.fear: The king's envoys asking why grain rotted in his barn while people starved on the far bank.
people.voice: Hearty, pressing, a hand on your shoulder. Talks as if you had already agreed.
people.looks: Early forties, big-bellied and sunburnt, cropped fair hair and a long moustache; a good blue cloak with a silver pin, riding boots, a bundle of split tally sticks.
knows: how much of the king's grain is to go downriver and to whom
the king's price and that the king's own grain sells below it
which boats on the strand are idle and why
when the host is to gather and what it will eat

ties.note: the clerk checks his tallies against the king's price and finds them, annoyingly, correct
lets the stone dealer fill his empty boats, which is not strictly the king's business
she says he steals carts; he says the king's wine does not wait for pots
the count's steward at Dorestad: they cut their tallies the same way and trust each other's sticks
delivers the king's grain into the count's district and wants the count's word that it was sold at the price
promised the bishop of Traiectum a cargo for the poor before harvest, and has the grain but not the boat
counts off every boat the steward at the Ruhr mouth sends up and writes to ask about each one short; Raginhard writes back one line
Gundhart of Mogontia has lent him a hull more than once and been paid in the king's grain, to the sack
in the vintage weeks the king's wine and Liutwin's want the same carts, the same hulls and the same three days of dry weather
a boatload of the king's barley meant for the Scheldt came a week late in the hungry spring; the ale-wife there brewed thin and told every skipper whose boat it was

lines.greet: A boat! Four men and a dry hold? God sent you. The king's grain, to Traiectum, and I pay in grain. When can you load?
lines.greet_again: My Frisian! You carried for me before and not a sack was light. I told them so at Deutz. I have more. I always have more.
rumour: The king's grain goes at two pennies for oats... no, I have it wrong, the clerk will tell you. Less than the top price, that is the point.
A man in the smiths' row offered me double for rye, to be fetched after dark. I said the king's grain does not see well at night.
The host eats before anyone. If you hear where it gathers, buy salt meat there in April and sell it in May. I did not tell you that.
lines.saying: A full barn in a hungry year is not wealth. It is a question somebody will ask you.
lines.farewell: Go on, go on, the water is good. And count the sacks at the other end in front of a priest.

people.source: invented; the spine's steward (hungry_years). Deutz as a royal estate: de.wikipedia Kastell Deutz. The king's own grain sold below the top price: Synod of Frankfurt 794 c. 4 (chronicle_793.json).

people.name: Bero
people.trait: A blade smith who deals in other smiths' work as well as his own. Careful, incurious by policy, proud of his welds.
people.want: Silver by weight, no names, and his blades on the hips of men who know what they are worth.
people.fear: The king's men with a list, and a customer who talks.
people.voice: Low and even. Speaks of blades as 'iron' and of buyers as 'a friend'. Never asks where you are going.
people.looks: About forty, spare and burn-scarred on the forearms, dark hair tied back, singed eyebrows; a leather apron, bare arms, a folding balance in a wooden case in his shirt.
knows: which smiths weld a name into the blade and which blades with that name are false
the law: no mail out of the realm, a blade to a count's man and to no stranger
what a sword fetches by the law's reckoning and what it fetches beyond the Eider
how a long bundle lies under ballast so a pole does not find it

ties.note: the clerk has wanted to see behind his hurdles for five years
has drunk at her fire every night for ten years and never said so
a blade travels well in a boatload of querns; neither man has ever mentioned it
the Dorestad skipper is his oldest carrier and the one he trusts least
the dealer at Sliesthorp paid for twelve blades and received ten
says the king's own Wendish ally sends for iron and it would be disloyal to refuse (from 798)
the Frisian comb-maker on the Scheldt will saw antler with no blade but Bero's; one saw goes down river each spring and a comb comes back, which Bero has given to nobody yet
the steward's men at the head of the Hellweg turn out every eastbound pack; Bero has lost two bundles there and the names of two carriers

lines.greet: Scythes, knives, boat nails. That is what I sell. If you want something longer you have come to the wrong shed. Come back at dusk.
lines.greet_again: You. Good. You did not talk, or I would have heard. I weigh, you carry. No coin: coin has a king's face on it.
rumour: A sword with its scabbard stands for seven solidi in the old law. North of the Danes' wall a friend gives three times that, in cut silver.
There is a smith upriver who welds his name into the iron. Already I see blades with his name that he never touched. Bend it before you buy.
They have forbidden mail to merchants now. Mail was always forbidden. What is new is that somebody means it.
lines.saying: I do not ask a nail which boat it will hold together.
lines.farewell: Lay it along the keel, stones on top, fleeces on the stones. And if the toll man's pole goes deep, you never saw me.

people.source: invented; the spine's dealer who asks no questions (swords_north). Sword with scabbard at 7 solidi: Lex Ribuaria 40 (36) c. 11. The ban: Herstal 779 c. 20; the capitulary for the missi of 803; Thionville 805 c. 7. The name welded into blades is the Ulfberht mark, 9th to 11th century, with many imitations.

people.name: Adaltrud
people.trait: Keeps the ale-house in the wall tower: remembers every face and every debt, and is the one person on the strand who is told everything.
people.want: Her house full and quiet, the tower roof mended, and her daughter Hiltrud married to a man who does not work on the water.
people.fear: Fire, the river in flood through her door, and soldiers quartered on her.
people.voice: Warm, quick and unsurprised. Calls every boatman 'my son' and remembers what he drank.
people.looks: Early thirties, tall and strong-armed, a broad calm face, fair plaits under a linen head cloth; an undyed apron over a green dress, a ladle, a bunch of tally sticks on a nail behind her.
knows: who is on the strand, who left this morning and what they were carrying
which boatmen want hiring and which are not worth it
what is said in the smiths' row after dark, and by whom
the height of the river by the third step of her door

ties.note: her mother's brother; she feeds him and he baptises whoever she tells him needs it
knows exactly why he comes every night and is waiting to see if he will ever say it
buys her cups and her gossip, and pays full price only for the gossip
the tower is the bishop's wall; she pays the clerk a rent in ale and in what she overhears, chosen with care
the only house on the Rhine where the big Saxon sits with his back to the door
the Northman sets her a riddle each visit and she has answered every one but the first
the ale-wife on the Frisians' shore at Mogontia says the tower waters its ale; Adaltrud says Ratburg's news is a week old when it is poured. They trade both by every barge
the ale-wife at the Ruhr mouth sends the price of malt and the names of bad payers up by the barge men, and gets the same back

lines.greet: Mind the step, my son, the Romans built it for taller men. Ale is a penny the pitcher. Where are you from, and is your boat dry?
lines.greet_again: There he is. The bench by the fire, your cup is the one with the chip. Your Saxon was asking for you, in his way, by not asking.
rumour: Two boats went down at first light, very low in the water, and nobody loaded them by day. I notice things. I do not say them to clerks.
The river is at my second step. At the third I move the ale upstairs; at the fourth I move myself. Do not leave your boat on a short rope.
The steward was in, shouting for hulls. He pays in grain and he pays what he says. This year grain is better than silver.
lines.saying: A tower stood here five hundred years to keep people out. It took me one winter to make them want to come in.
lines.farewell: God go with you. I will keep your cup. Nobody else drinks from the chipped one; I tell them it is unlucky.

people.source: invented; the house is the game's (?). After her the house is kept by her daughter Hiltrud and Hiltrud's children, who keep the chipped cup for the merchant's heirs.

people.name: Liutwin
people.trait: Head of a house that sells Rhenish wine by the cask and the green glass to drink it from: smooth, exact, never seen to hurry, and never seen to carry anything himself.
people.want: One buyer in every palace cellar from Noviomagus to the sea, and the potter's widow on the next pitch struck dumb for a single market day.
people.fear: A cask that turns on the way to a king's table with his mark burned in the head of it.
people.voice: Soft and unhurried. Lets you taste first, names the price after, and holds the cup up to the light while he does it.
people.looks: About forty-five, tall and narrow, a trimmed grey-brown beard, a long tunic of good dark red wool, clean hands, a small green glass beaker hung in a net at his belt.
knows: what a cask of this year's wine and last year's costs here, at Mogontia and at Dorestad
which palace and abbey cellarers buy ahead and which of them pay
glass: beakers, bowls and panes, who blows them on the river strip and how to pack them for the sea
a verse in Latin about a black wrinkled thing that stings the tongue, which he cannot read and has by heart

ties.note: the palace cellarer at Noviomagus has bought from this house every autumn for twenty years; he is the Cologne wine house Ratbert means
buys the upper river's wine from the Frisian at Mogontia when his own growers are short, and resents every cask
she sells wine in clay on the next pitch and tells his buyers that glass is for people who want to see what they are being cheated of
the king's steward takes the carts and the hulls in the vintage weeks; Liutwin pays the carters a penny more and says nothing
her storehouse on the dam at Dorestad holds his casks between the river boats and the sea boats (?)
a Svea trader ordered forty green beakers through a Frisian and paid half; the other half and the beakers are both still on the Rhine

lines.greet: Taste before you ask the price. No, hold it to the light first. Clay hides a wine. Glass tells you the truth about it.
lines.greet_again: The small boat from Dorestad. The last casks arrived sound, I hear. I always hear. How many this time?
rumour: The palace at Noviomagus buys ahead every autumn. If the king winters there, wine at Dorestad is dear by Christmas. Ask where he winters.
A Frisian at Mogontia keeps a cask he will not sell. I have offered three times. A man with one cask he will not sell has a hundred he will.
Northmen pay for a green beaker what a Frank pays for a cask. Pack them in bran, not straw. Straw is for pots.
lines.riddle: A monk paid me in a verse once. Black outside, wrinkled, bites the tongue, and kings want it at table. Answer the glass one first and it is yours.
lines.saying: Wine is the only cargo a buyer thanks you for twice: once when it comes, and once when it is gone.
lines.farewell: Go down gently. A cask does not mind the river. It minds the man who drops it on the strand at the other end.

people.source: invented (Liut- and -win are attested Frankish name parts); the id is the one places/noviomagus.json ties to. Rhenish wine in casks from Colonia to Dorestad and the palaces (Design/economy_and_trade.md); glass working on the river strip (the Heumarkt dig (?)); glass beakers from the Rhine found from Dorestad to Birka. He is the 'dealer in Rhenish glass' who holds the pepper riddle (riddles_793.json riddle_aldhelm_40_piper), the last link of the set salt_to_pepper. After 817 the house goes on under his sons.

people.name: Hadebald
people.trait: Archbishop after Hildebold: a builder and a lender of books, more often in his city than his master was, and generous with what the church can spare, boats included.
people.want: Saint Peter's roofed again after the fire, its books counted and back on their shelves, and the mission to the Danes sent off decently.
people.fear: The quarrel of the emperor's sons reaching the Rhine, and having to say whose archbishop he is.
people.voice: Plain and kind, with a builder's habit of asking how long a thing will take and then halving the answer.
people.looks: About fifty in 826, broad and ruddy, a grey tonsure, a good brown travelling cloak over white, a mason's cord and a book list on one thong at his belt.
knows: which of the hundred and seventy-five books of Saint Peter's are lent out, and to whom
what the emperor's court has decided about the Danes and their baptised king
the price of lead, glass and oak for a church roof
who is abbot of the two houses at Ganda and how many days a boat takes from there to the Main

ties.note: gave the young monk and the Danish king a good boat with two cabins for the road to Dorestad in 826
both men of the emperor Louis's court; Einhard's letters and his wax for the Main go past this strand, and the bishop's clerks pass them through (?)
the archbishop of Mogontia baptised the Danish king; Colonia gave him the boat. Each see remembers its own half of the story
inherits the old clerk with the lists, the seal and the mint's rule, and for five years is corrected by him

lines.greet: A Dorestad boat. Good. You people know the lower river better than my clerks do. How many days to the sea at this water?
lines.greet_again: You again, and the boat dry. I lent a king a boat once and he would not get out of it. Yours I only want for a week.
rumour: A king of the Danes was baptised upriver at midsummer. He goes home down this river with a monk. I have found them a boat with two cabins.
We have counted the books: a hundred and seventy-five. Nine are lent. I know where seven are. If you pass Ganda, ask the abbot's steward about a psalter.
The church burned in my master's last years. I am told it will be finished in mine. Builders say so to every bishop.
lines.saying: Lend a book and you learn who your friends are. Lend a boat and you learn who the king's are.
lines.farewell: Go with God. If you overtake a boat with two cabins, greet the monk in the smaller one. He will need friends where he is going.

people.source: Hadebald, archbishop of Colonia 819 to 841 (de.wikipedia Liste der Erzbischöfe und Bischöfe von Köln, by way of the dossier); the boat with two cabins given to Harald and Anskar in 826: Rimbert, Vita Anskarii c. 7 (tr. Robinson 1921); the 175 books listed in 833 (de.wikipedia Erzbischöfliche Diözesan- und Dombibliothek Köln). His birth year is not known (0). His looks, his character and his words are invented; whether he and Einhard dealt with each other is not recorded (?).

people.name: Bruno
people.trait: King Otto's youngest brother, archbishop and duke of Lotharingia at once: learned, sleepless, a man who reads on horseback and rules a town between two chapters.
people.want: The market, the mint and the toll in the church's hand; monks at Saint Pantaleon and a chapter on the old island; and his brother's kingdom quiet west of the Rhine.
people.fear: That he will be remembered as a duke who said Mass, and not the other way about.
people.voice: Quick and exact, Saxon under the Latin. Asks what a thing costs, what it weighs and who else knows.
people.looks: About thirty, slight and pale, short fair hair under a plain cap, a dark wool cloak with no gold on it but the ring, a book in a saddle bag and ink on his cuff.
knows: who holds court, market, mint and toll in every town of Lotharingia, since he appoints them
what the king his brother wants from the Rhine towns this year
the price of stone, lead and bell metal, because he is building in three places
Greek, a little, and where on the river a book in it can be found (?)

ties.note: the bishop of Traiectum schooled him from the age of four; Bruno sends him books and, once, the relics he asked for
the Mogontia merchant who went to the Greek emperor for the king drops a Greek word in every sentence; Bruno is the one man on the river who answers in it (?)

lines.greet: A house of the old Dorestad line. I was schooled at Traiectum; I know what your river was. Sit. What does the toll at my gate cost you?
lines.greet_again: You told me the truth about the toll last time. My officer did not. One of you has since changed his reckoning.
rumour: I am setting a chapter on the old island above the market. Your boats will lie under its windows. Monks hear everything; mind what you shout.
The king my brother has beaten the Hungarians on the Lech. There will be silver from the east this year and peace on the roads to carry it.
The market is the church's now, and the mint. A merchant who dislikes that may say so to me. It is quicker than saying it to each other.
lines.saying: A duke may be obeyed without being read. A bishop may be read without being obeyed. I am trying to manage both.
lines.farewell: Go safely. Greet Bishop Balderik if you pass Traiectum, and tell him the boy still knows his declensions.

people.source: Bruno (Brun), born 925, King Otto I's brother; archbishop of Colonia and duke of Lotharingia from 953; from his day the archbishop held court, market, mint and toll; a chapter at Saint Martin's about 960 and an abbey at Saint Pantaleon; died at Reims on 11 October 965 (de.wikipedia Brun (Köln); Groß St. Martin; St. Pantaleon, by way of the dossier). Schooled at Traiectum under Bishop Balderik: places/traiectum.json. The Lech, 955: chronicle. That he had Greek is Ruotger's Life, from memory (?). The id is the one places/traiectum.json ties to. His looks and words are invented.

stories.title: A hand-breadth either way
stories.summary: While the kings quarrel and the English trade is shut, Meginher the stone dealer has two hundred Mayen roughouts and no idea what size the English king asked for. He will pay for the answer, and so will his rival.
stories.picture: A heavy man in a leather apron holding a notched measuring stick across a stack of round black stones on dark earth, a Roman wall behind him and a small boat's mast beyond it.

beats.text: Meginher says the English king has asked for black stones and nobody on the Rhine knows the size. He cuts a tally: the true measure, brought back, is worth a boatload of finished querns at his cost.
Finished querns for the English trade stand unsold on the dam. Thiadbod offers silver, now, for whatever you learn across the sea, provided he hears it before the man at Colonia does.
The wic-reeve Wighelm, for a gift and a story, says what the king's mills want: the stones' width shown on his own staff, in English hand-breadths. He lets you cut it on your stick.
Gervold's clerk has seen the letters. He will not show them, but looks at the notches on your stick and says nothing, which from a toll clerk is agreement.

Gundhart the grain man has Meginher's millstones on his Main boats and Meginher's worry with them: the stone dealer has not cut a quern since the ports shut. The upper mill wants two stones before harvest, whatever the English want.

Adalwin counts the black stones in every hull bound for the abbeys at Ganda and takes his tenth in querns. He has a stack by the toll post, all of one width, and says nobody has yet complained of it but Meginher.
You lay the stick on Meginher's stack. He is a hand-breadth out on every stone, on the side that can still be cut.

endings.how: You brought Meginher the reeve's measure and told no one else.
endings.text: He recuts the whole yard. The week the kings make peace his stones are on the dam at Dorestad and Thiadbod's are the wrong size. Meginher keeps a stone back for you every year after.
endings.reward: A boatload of querns at his cost (about 240 pennies' worth at Dorestad); the unlock colonia.stone_credit; Meginher a fast friend, and his son after him.

endings.how: You sold the measure to Thiadbod first and to Meginher after.
endings.text: Both yards cut to the same size and the price of querns in England falls by a third in a season. Each man works out, within the year, where the other heard it.
endings.reward: About 150 pennies in silver from the two of them; Meginher cool, Thiadbod amused; querns sell worse at Lundenwic for three years.

endings.how: You never crossed the sea and gave him a measure of your own invention.
endings.text: He cuts to it. In 796 the first boatload comes back from the Thames unsold. He does not shout. He has the returned stones stacked where you tie up.
endings.reward: The price of one boatload, taken once. Meginher wary for life; Gerhild doubles her prices to you for a year and tells you why.

stories.reward: A stone dealer's credit on the Rhine, or quick silver and two men who know what you are.

stories.title: The names on the list
stories.summary: Colonia is the king's crossing place. In 799 and again in 804 whole Saxon households wait on the bank to be sent into Francia, an old priest reads them the vow again, and the clerk's lists go back to 785: Brunger's brother is on one.
stories.picture: Families sitting on bundles on a river bank under a high Roman wall, a red-faced old priest reading from a small book, a thin clerk beside him with a wax tablet, a broad ferry waiting.

beats.text: Brunger will not go near the crossing. Adaltrud says the clerk's lists hold every hostage who came down the river since the Saxons first submitted, and that the clerk can be asked, if one knows how.
The bank is full of households under guard. Erkanbert reads the vow in Saxon; they answer. He asks whether your boat could take the old and the children upriver, so they need not walk.
Hrotbert will read the roll of 785 to a man who has done the bishop a service, or to one who brings Erkanbert's word. A boy from the Weser, given to a lord of the Alemans: sent on by Mogontia.
At the Ruhr mouth a column comes down the Hellweg on foot. Raginhard the steward wants hulls. One of the guards served in the south and knows the lord's name on the roll.

In the court kitchen Hathuswith hears what the roll at Colonia said and nods: twelve Weser boys, the year of the vow, by boat to the bishops. She adds what no roll has, that one of them would not answer to his new name.

At mid-Lent the hostages kept in the south are brought to Mogontia. Otbert has Hrotbert's roll on the table beside his own list, and the brother stands between them: a grown man who speaks the Alemans' tongue and has a master.

endings.how: You carried the old and the children upriver for the priest and asked the clerk through him.
endings.text: Erkanbert stands beside you at the gate and Hrotbert reads the entry aloud, twice. Brunger hears it from the strand. He says nothing until the boat is under way, and then one proverb.
endings.reward: Sets sx_brother_trail; the text saxon_vow for the chest; Erkanbert and Brunger fast friends; the church remembers the deed.

endings.how: You paid Hrotbert's price: a service to the bishop, a letter carried to Traiectum and an answer brought back.
endings.text: The clerk keeps his word to the letter. He reads the entry and no more, and writes down that you asked. Your name is now on a list too.
endings.reward: Sets sx_brother_trail; the unlock colonia.bishops_letter; Hrotbert friendly, and from then on he asks what you carry before the gate does.

endings.how: You hired your boat to the king's officer and carried the households as cargo.
endings.text: It pays in the king's silver and it is lawful. Brunger rows the whole way without a word and on the strand at Colonia he asks to be paid off.
endings.reward: About 120 pennies and the king's men's good word on the Rhine; Brunger leaves the boat unless the brother's trail is already found; Erkanbert does not greet you again.

endings.text: The households go south on foot. The lists stay in their chest. In 805 Brunger hears of the mid-Lent order from a stranger and asks why nobody told him sooner.
endings.reward: Nothing gained or lost in silver. Brunger's want can still be met at Mogontia, late and harder.

stories.reward: The trail to Brunger's brother and an old priest's friendship, or the king's silver and an empty seat at the oars.

stories.title: The king's grain
stories.summary: The Rhine is the road grain comes down. In the hungry years the king's estate at Deutz sells his own grain below the top price and the steward has no hulls to move it; a man in the smiths' row offers far more, for delivery after dark.
stories.picture: Sacks going down a plank into a small boat at dusk, a big sunburnt man with tally sticks counting aloud, and in the shadow of the wall a second man holding up a purse without a word.

beats.text: Wido wants hulls: the king's grain to Traiectum, where the bishop is ordered to feed the starving. He pays one sack in eight, and cuts a tally for the count of sacks. In the same weeks he has barley for the Scheldt, where the ale-wife at Andoverpis is brewing thin.

The grain itself comes down the Main. Otbert lists the hulls at Mogontia and Gundhart lends one; what is loaded there at the king's price is counted off by Wido on the strand at Colonia, sack for sack.

The king's barley is opened on the selling bank at Andoverpis with the priest watching the measure. Wido's tally stick is broken in two there, and Ermentrud keeps her half on the rafter with the rest.
A dealer offers twice the king's price for the same sacks, set down below the town after dark. He says grain has no memory of whose it was.
Bishop Hamacar's people count the sacks at the church door in front of a priest. The poor are already standing there.
A better year. Wido settles his tallies. If the count was right he has told them so at Deutz, and the king's wine can go in your hold at Martinmas.

endings.how: You delivered every sack to Traiectum and took the steward's eighth.
endings.text: The bishop's clerk writes the count; Wido's tally matches it to the sack. He tells the story at Deutz with his hand on someone else's shoulder.
endings.reward: Sets hy_fed_poor; an eighth of the cargo in grain, worth most where bread is dearest; the unlock colonia.kings_wine; Wido and Hamacar friendly.

endings.how: You set the sacks down below the town for the dealer's silver.
endings.text: It is the best price of your life. Wido's tally comes up short at Traiectum and Hrotbert, who can count, begins to ask which boat it was.
endings.reward: About twice the cargo's worth in silver by weight; sets hy_sold_dear; Wido shuns you, and the count's men at Dorestad may ask about it.

endings.how: You delivered the count whole and left your own eighth at the church door as well.
endings.text: Hamacar asks your name and has it written. Erkanbert hears of it at Colonia before you are back, and for once has nothing blunt to say.
endings.reward: Sets hy_fed_poor; no profit on the voyage; prayers said for the house at Traiectum and Colonia, and a deed the church remembers in both towns.

stories.reward: The king's steward as a patron and his wine in your hold, or one very good night's silver.

stories.title: Iron at dusk
stories.summary: A blade may be sold to a count's man and to no stranger. Bero, at the closed shed in the smiths' row, sells to a friend, for silver by weight, and wants a quiet boat to carry long bundles to the Dorestad water and beyond.
stories.picture: A spare man with burn-scarred arms weighing cut silver on a folding balance by a banked forge, a long bundle wrapped in greased wool on the anvil block, dusk in the doorway.

beats.text: Bero shows one blade: pattern in the iron like running water. He names no buyer. Ten of them to the inland water north of Dorestad, and he weighs out the carrying fee before you answer. A smaller bundle goes the other way first, a day down the river, to a man who lodges with the smith at Diusburg.

The man on the smith's bench at Diusburg takes Bero's bundle without unwrapping it and weighs out cut silver. From 805 the steward's watch at the head of the Hellweg turns out every pack that leaves his door going east.
At Mogontia the same iron is sold under a king's man's eye. The smith there knows Bero's weld when he sees it and says only that it came a long way up the river to be looked at.
The toll man's pole goes into the ballast. Under the stones and fleeces lies what you were told to lay along the keel.
On the Almere shore, out of the count's sight, a boat with a northern stem comes alongside at night. A name is given, once: the man at Sliesthorp who is owed two blades.
Hrotbert has your name on a tablet. He reads you the rule on arms slowly, and asks what is behind the hurdles in the smiths' row. He would rather have the smith than the carrier.
An abbey's steward has old mail to be rid of and cannot say so. Bero will not touch church iron. He tells you who would.

endings.how: You carried the bundles north and kept your mouth shut.
endings.text: Bero weighs out the second half of the fee without counting twice. After the third run he tells you, unasked, which blades with a name in them are false.
endings.reward: Sets sw_ran_blades and sw_buyer_known; about 200 pennies' weight of silver a run; the unlock colonia.bend_the_blade; one more search you must pass each voyage.

endings.how: You said no and said nothing to the clerk.
endings.text: Bero nods as if you had refused a cup of ale. He sells you scythes and boat nails at a fair price for the rest of his life, and Adaltrud keeps your cup.
endings.reward: Nothing gained, nothing owed; tools and nails here a tenth cheaper, because a man who can keep quiet is worth keeping.

endings.how: You told Hrotbert what is behind the hurdles.
endings.text: The king's men take the shed apart and find scythes. Bero is fined for something else. Hrotbert has what he wanted for five years and gives you a letter with the bishop's seal.
endings.reward: The unlock colonia.bishops_letter; clears sw_marked; the smiths' row is closed to you, Adaltrud serves you last, and Thiadbod hears of it at Dorestad.

stories.reward: A dangerous steady income and a smith's secret, or a seal and a strand that has gone quiet around you.

stories.title: Gates, bars and locks
stories.summary: In the winter of 881 the Northmen who took the lower river come up to Colonia. A ransom is paid after Epiphany and the town burns all the same; the clergy go to Mogontia with the treasures and the saints. Two years later the walls are mended with gates, bars and locks, and the fleet goes by.
stories.picture: A river boat pushing off in winter dusk with a draped chest and two priests aboard, smoke and a red glow over a long Roman wall behind, snow on the strand.

beats.text: The Northmen hold the palace at Noviomagus and winter there. A merchant who has seen them counts the ships and knows they will not stay below the hills another year.

It is the same army. Beaten at Saucourt, it refits its ships on the wrights' strand at Ganda and goes on to the Meuse; a merchant who watched the planking there knows how many hulls will be on the Rhine before the frost.
A day below Colonia the Frisian Thiadward has heard the same count and begun to bury what he owns. He asks every boat from upriver whether the wall at Colonia has gates yet.
If you bring the count of ships upriver before the frost, the house in the tower believes you first and the canons last. The strand empties of boats in a week.
The canons are packing Saint Peter's treasure and the saints' bodies for Mogontia. They need a boat that can go against the stream in winter, and men who will tow.

At Mogontia the canons and nuns of Colonia and Bonn live as guests of Archbishop Liutbert, with their chests. News comes up of the ransom paid, and then of the fire. In 883 Liutbert himself goes out with a few men and takes plunder back from the Northmen.
The wall is mended and the gate has new oak leaves, an iron bar and a lock. Nothing stands inside but timber roofs. The people who are back ask what a man could give toward the rest.

endings.how: You towed the canons' chests to Mogontia in winter.
endings.text: The bodies of the saints lie at Mogontia while Colonia burns. When they come home in 883 the house that carried them is named at the altar, and its heirs are greeted at the gate by name.
endings.reward: A relic's keeping remembered: the unlock colonia.named_at_the_altar; the archbishop's toll forgiven the house for a generation; a deed the church remembers on the whole Rhine.

endings.how: You brought the count of ships up from Noviomagus before the frost.
endings.text: The boats, the wine and most of the people are upriver when the fire comes. The ransom is still paid, by the men who stayed, and still wasted. Nobody on the strand forgets who came first.
endings.reward: Sets df_warned; the ale-house and the strand families fast friends to the house; a free berth and a free tow whenever the heirs come.

endings.how: You came after the fire and bought what the Northmen had not carried off.
endings.text: Lead from the roofs, scorched casks, a bell with a crack in it: all cheap, all sold by people with nothing else. It is trade. The sellers remember your face as the one that was not burned.
endings.reward: A hold of lead, iron and church metal at a third of its worth; feeling at Colonia falls for a generation.

stories.reward: A name read at the altar of Saint Peter's, or a cheap cargo and a long memory against you.

stories.title: One weight in every market
stories.summary: From the summer of 794 the king's new penny is to be taken in every place, town and market, and the bishop's clerk at the mint of Colonia reads the rule aloud to anyone who argues. He also has a bag of pennies that are not what they say, some of them with Mogontia's name on them, and wants it carried up the river sealed, to be weighed by the one moneyer whose scale he trusts as little as his own.
stories.picture: A cellar lit by a charcoal hearth: a thin clerk holding a small linen bag with a wax seal on its knot over a balance, a pan of clipped pennies on the table, and a merchant with his hand not yet out.

beats.text: Hrotbert reads the rule on the new penny, then shows a coin that is tin under the skin, sent by Sigimar of Dorestad out of an English purse. He has thirty doubtful pennies in a sealed bag for Madalger at Mogontia and asks whether your boat goes up.

Madalger breaks the seal on the cloth and weighs all thirty without a word. Eleven are light, and nine of those are of a die he knows. He taps the table once and writes the count on the bag, for the clerk at Colonia and for nobody else.
Sigimar at Dorestad hears from a skipper what the scale at Mogontia said before either mint has written to him. He asks who carried the bag, and whether the seal was whole.

For eleven years the port at Ganda strikes the western king's pennies with its own name on them. A Colonia man lays one on his folding scale at a house door there, nods, and says the old clerk would have liked to see it.

On a stall by the river gate at Mogontia lies silver with no king's face on it at all, struck at Samarkand, and it is weighed more fairly than any penny. A hundred and seventy years of one weight in every market, and the best silver on the Rhine is still sold by the scale.

endings.how: You carried the bag up sealed and Madalger's count back down, and read neither.
endings.text: Two clerks and a moneyer who trust nobody have found one carrier they need not weigh. Hrotbert writes your boat on a list he has not shown you, with a mark beside it that he has given to four men in thirty years.
endings.reward: Silver for the carrying (about 20 pennies); the mints at Colonia and Mogontia test and change your silver without the usual loss; Madalger's lesson with the nick and the scale (flag sv_scale); Hrotbert and Madalger friendly, and Sigimar hears of it.

endings.how: You saw whose die the light pennies were struck from, and told Madalger quietly before the count was written.
endings.text: He looks at you a long time, then at his own right hand. The count that goes down the river says eleven light, die unknown. In spring there is a new man at the second anvil in the mint at Mogontia.
endings.reward: Madalger a fast friend, and his son after him; a dirham shown and explained when one comes (flag sv_first_dirham); Hrotbert never learns why the bad Mogontia pennies stopped, and it annoys him for the rest of his life.

endings.how: You broke the seal below the town and spent the doubtful pennies at markets where nobody weighs.
endings.text: Thirty pennies go as good coin on the lower river. One comes back to Colonia in a toll bag within the year, and Hrotbert knows every coin he ever sealed.
endings.reward: Thirty pennies, once; flag sv_old_coin; both mints weigh every coin you bring, slowly, in front of other people; Sigimar at Dorestad is told by letter.

stories.reward: Two mints that take your silver without loss and a moneyer's lesson, or a moneyer's lifelong friendship, or thirty pennies and your name on the wrong list.

works.name: A vault under the wall
works.what: A Roman cellar on the river side of the town, cleared of rubble and given an oak door and a lock: cool the year round, dry above the third flood step, and big enough for forty casks.
works.needs: The bishop's clerk must lease it, since the wall and what lies against it are the church's: three visits, or a service done for Hrotbert or his successors.
works.gives: Wine bought at Martinmas can lie here until it is dear (store); pots and querns can wait for a full cargo; goods in the vault are safe from the river and, in 881, are lost with the town unless moved.
works.picture: A barrel-vaulted Roman cellar with casks on timber cradles, a man with a lamp turning a big iron key in an oak door.
works.source: Great St Martin stands over Roman warehouses on the old harbour island (de.wikipedia Groß St. Martin); the use of a Roman vault by a merchant is the game's (?).

works.name: A timber hard on the strand
works.what: Oak piles driven into the gravel and decked with split logs, with a post to tie to, so that a boat can be loaded over a plank at any height of the river.
works.needs: Low water in late summer, and the good will of the strand: Adaltrud's word or Wido's.
works.gives: Loading here takes half the time and no porters are needed for casks; the boat rides out a spate without being hauled up. Burned in 881 and to be paid for again after 883.
works.picture: Men driving an oak pile with a wooden beetle from a raft, the river low and brown, the towered wall behind.
works.source: No quay is recorded at Colonia in these years (?); the Heumarkt's first laid surface is dated by its timbers to 957 (de.wikipedia Heumarkt). Timber jetties of this kind are known from Dorestad.

works.name: A book for Saint Peter's chest
works.what: The price of the skins, the ink and a scribe's winter, for a book the church lacks: a psalter, a book of the canons, or the lives of the saints who lie outside the wall. The giver's name is written at the end.
works.needs: An audience with the bishop or his clerk, and a copy to work from: borrowed at Traiectum or Mogontia, or carried from across the sea.
works.gives: The scribes read to you and let you copy (read_text and copy_text without a gift); the bishop's letter is yours for the asking; your name stands in a book that is counted in 833.
works.picture: A scribe at a slanted desk in window light, a half-written page before him and a deer skin stretched on a frame behind.
works.source: 175 books listed at Saint Peter's in 833 (de.wikipedia Erzbischöfliche Diözesan- und Dombibliothek Köln). A lay giver's name in a colophon is the game's (?).

works.name: A share in the river gate
works.what: Oak for the leaves, iron for the bar and a smith's month for the lock of the gate onto the strand, when the walls are restored after the burning.
works.needs: The years just after the fire, and to be known here: a friend on the strand, or a name at the altar.
works.gives: The house's boats are let in at the river gate after dark and in time of alarm; the toll bench knows the house; when the Northmen pass again the house's goods are inside the wall.
works.picture: Two carpenters hanging a heavy new oak gate leaf in a scorched Roman arch while a smith fits a long iron bar.
works.source: Annales Fuldenses 883: Colonia rebuilt, its walls restored 'with gates, bars and locks' (our rendering). Townsmen paying a share is the game's (?).

works.name: A house plot by the market
works.what: A strip of ground between the market and the river in the suburb that is now inside the walls, with leave to build a timber house on a stone footing and to keep a boat before it.
works.needs: The archbishop holds the market: his officer's leave, and a year's trade here without a quarrel over toll.
works.gives: The house may winter at Colonia and trade as a townsman; a ship can be built to order here; the Colonia men count you among their own when they sail to the Thames.
works.picture: A narrow timber house going up on a stone footing among others like it, the market in front and a mast showing over the roofs behind.
works.source: The river suburb taken into the town about 950; the archbishop lord of market, mint and toll from 953 (de.wikipedia Geschichte der Stadt Köln; Brun). A street 'inter Frisones' about 1100 hints at a Frisian quarter (?). Merchants with their own ships, 1074 (de.wikipedia Anno II.).

ships.how: built to order over a winter | bought second-hand
ships.note: The working boat of the middle Rhine: flat-bottomed, drifting down with the stream under a steering sweep and towed back up by men or oxen. Built on the bank below Saint Kunibert's from oak of the hills behind the town.
ships.picture: A long flat-bottomed barge loaded with casks and tall jars in straw, drifting downstream past a towered wall, one man at a long sweep.
ships.source: River craft at Colonia (dossier section 4); hired rowers in 1062 (de.wikipedia Anno II.). The yard is the game's (?).

ships.note: The older kind of river freighter, hewn from one great oak and spread with planks: cheap, heavy, and sold off the strand when a boatman grows too old to tow.
ships.picture: A dark, blunt-ended boat hewn from a single trunk with a plank added to each side, half full of black querns.
ships.source: Design/content/ships.md, the Utrecht type's forerunners on the Rhine (?).

ships.note: A two-man plank skiff for errands across to Deutz and for lightering casks out to a boat that cannot come in at low water.
ships.picture: A small flat skiff with two men and one cask crossing a wide brown river toward a square stone fort.
ships.source: The Deutz crossing (de.wikipedia Kastell Deutz); the class is from ship_classes_793.json.

ships.note: The bishop's own boat, with a deck house fore and aft, lent or hired with her crew to those the church wishes well. In 826 one such carried a Danish king and a monk to Dorestad, a cabin each.
ships.picture: A handsome river boat with two small cabins, a cross at her stem, a king's man leaning in one doorway and a monk reading in the other.
ships.source: Rimbert, Vita Anskarii c. 7 (tr. Robinson 1921): the boat Bishop Hadebald gave had two cabins.

ships.how: built to order over a winter
ships.note: By about 1000 the men of the Rhine towns sail to London in their own ships. A townsman with a plot by the market can have a sea-going hull laid down here and take her down the river on the spring water.
ships.picture: A deep, broad sea-going ship on the stocks on a river bank, far too large for the barges beside her, townsmen in long cloaks watching.
ships.source: IV Æthelred 2: 'the men of the Emperor who came in their own ships' (Thorpe 1840); merchants of Colonia with their own ships in 1074 (de.wikipedia Anno II.). Building them at Colonia itself is a guess (?).

sayings.text: The new pennies are to be taken in every place, in every town and in every market, if they bear the king's name and are of pure silver and full weight.
sayings.source: Synod of Frankfurt 794 c. 5 (MGH Capitularia I no. 28; our rendering, by way of spine.json)

sayings.text: If a man must pay a wergild, let him give a sword with its scabbard for seven solidi, a mail coat for twelve, a helmet for six.
sayings.source: Lex Ribuaria 40 (36) c. 11 (our rendering, after Design/economy_and_trade.md)

sayings.text: This year the town was built again, without its churches, and the walls set up with gates, bars and locks. On the strand they say: so now we are safe from everything but the weather and the archbishop.
sayings.source: Annales Fuldenses 883 (ed. Kurze 1891; our rendering); the second sentence invented in the period's manner

sayings.text: Down with the stream in four days, back against it in fourteen. The Rhine lends and the tow rope collects.
sayings.source: invented in the period's manner; the travel times are Design/research_trade_seasons_and_hints.md

sayings.text: Written in the margin of a book at Saint Peter's: The skin is hairy, the ink is thin, the day is short and the bishop is at court. Thank God, at least, for the last.
sayings.source: invented in the manner of the scribes' marginal complaints of the 9th century

sayings.text: A Frank asked a Frisian why his cloak was so short. So that I can see what my money is doing, said the Frisian.
sayings.source: invented in the period's manner, after Notker, Gesta Karoli I.34, on the short Frisian cloaks

sayings.text: A riddle of the market: I am two and lie one upon the other. The upper turns and the lower sleeps; what comes between us is broken, and whole houses live on the breaking. Say what I am. (A quern.)
sayings.source: invented in the manner of the Exeter and Aldhelm riddles

sayings.text: The Romans built the wall. The saints were buried outside it. That tells you what each of them thought of the town.
sayings.source: invented in the period's manner; burial outside the walls in the Roman cemeteries (dossier section 6)

sayings.text: At Colonia even the devils had seats in church, and kept them five hundred years.
sayings.source: invented in the period's manner, after Annales Fuldenses 870: spirits heard grieving that they must leave seats held so long

easter_eggs.text: In 826 the bishop's boat goes down the river with a Danish king in one cabin and a young monk named Anskar in the other. The king liked the boat so well that he moved in; with a cabin each, they became friends before Dorestad.

Set in the wall of the church of the Holy Virgins, north of the town, is a stone cut in good Roman letters by one Clematius, who rebuilt the hall where the virgins died. In 793 nobody numbers them and nobody names them; the eleven thousand and Ursula come later.
easter_eggs.source: de.wikipedia St. Ursula (Köln); en.wikipedia Saint Ursula: 'thousands' in 848, 11,000 by the late 9th century, the name Ursula in the 10th

easter_eggs.text: The old kings' hall of the Romans stands roofless near the east wall with a crack down it a man can put his arm in. One wet winter in these years a great part of it will slide toward the Rhine. The boys bet on which year.
easter_eggs.source: de.wikipedia Praetorium (Köln): large parts slid toward the Rhine in the 8th or 9th century

easter_eggs.text: The bishop's small prayer book is bound in deer hide. Asked about it, he says a priest once wanted no more than that from a stranger who could have given gold. He does not say which of the two he was.
easter_eggs.source: the late legend of Hildebold and the king (de.wikipedia Hildebold von Köln)

easter_eggs.text: On the night before Saint Peter's was dedicated in 870, people near the church heard voices complaining bitterly that they were being turned out of seats they had held so long.
